output.title: Rollback is a backup, not the control
output.body:
Rollback plans sound tidy until you look at the actual workflow risk. For a small business owner, the real question is not “can we undo it later?” It is “what stops this automation from causing damage while it runs?” If the wrong reply goes out, a duplicate invoice is created, or a manual check gets skipped, rolling back afterward does not erase what already reached the inbox, the CRM, or the payment flow.

That is why rollback is not enough on its own. It returns you to the previous state. It does not stop bad data, bad answers, or bad decisions from propagating. The control has to come before commitment.

A practical next step is simple: pick one recurring workflow you might automate, write down the three worst failure modes—wrong data, missed items, and duplicates—and choose one human approval gate that would block the most damaging one before it is posted or sent. If you are testing invoice extraction, spot-check a few entries against the source documents before anything is posted. If the risk is money movement, keep human approval in place. That is not a rollback plan; it is a gate.

Bareni’s policy is that accounts and tools stay in the customer’s name, and finished code is handed over. That is no-lock-in positioning, not a warranty. In small business automation, the useful habit is still the same: control the workflow first, then decide whether it belongs there at all.
